\chapter{What You Put On}
\label{ch:la-ropa-y-el-zapato}
\hlchaptermodality{360}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say la ropa, el vestido, el zapato, el pantalón and el botón, and name what someone is wearing.}

Complete ES-C360-boton: name four things a person has on, and the one small thing that holds them shut.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la ropa]{la ropa — the clothes that started out as loot}

\label{lesson:ES-C360-ropa}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the litre}, then \emph{the weight}. (\emph{El litro}; \emph{el peso}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la tienda — the place where you go and get it.
  \item comprar — the verb you will pair with it constantly.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{RO-pa}, two beats with the weight on the first. The opening \emph{r} is trilled, rolled at the front of the mouth, not the soft English one. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la ropa} — \textquotedblleft{}clothes.\textquotedblright{}

This word begins with an armed band walking away from a burning village. Germanic \textbf{raupa} meant booty: the plunder, the pile you carry off. The verb standing beside it, \textbf{raupjan}, meant to pluck or to strip.

What did raiders actually take? Not stone, not furniture. Cloth — bolts of it, cloaks, coats. Cloth was light, valuable, and easy to sell on. So the word for loot narrowed to the word for cloth goods, and then narrowed again to the things a person puts on.

English holds the older end of the same root:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item to \textbf{rob} is to take the plunder, arriving through Old French \emph{rober};
  \item to \textbf{reave}, and to be \textbf{bereaved}, is to be stripped of something;
  \item German still has \emph{rauben}, to rob.
\end{itemize}

Here is the part worth carrying away. Old French \textbf{robe} also meant booty first, and it also drifted to mean a garment. Two languages, no contact between them on this point, and the same slide runs twice: what was taken becomes what is worn. Put on a \textbf{robe} and you are wearing spoils, in the same sense that \emph{ropa} is spoils.

One trap, and it catches beginners often: \emph{ropa} is not English \textbf{rope}. Rope is Old English \emph{rāp}, a wholly separate word that happens to have landed on nearly the same sounds.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name the whole category of what a person wears, in one word: \emph{la ropa}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la ropa}
  \item \emph{la ropa nueva}
  \item \emph{la ropa de la tienda}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Germanic \emph{raupa} mean before it meant clothes? (Plunder, booty.) And which English garment made the same slide on its own? (A \emph{robe}, which meant spoils first.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el vestido]{el vestido — the dress that is a past participle}

\label{lesson:ES-C360-vestido}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the weight}, then \emph{the clothes}. (\emph{El peso}; \emph{la ropa}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la fiesta — the occasion this word turns up at.
  \item la bolsa — another thing you carry or wear, already yours.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bes-TI-do}, three beats with the weight on the middle one. The \emph{v} is made with the lips of a \emph{b}, and the \emph{d} between vowels goes soft, close to the \emph{th} of \emph{this}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el vestido} — \textquotedblleft{}the dress.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{vestis} was a garment and \textbf{vestīre} was to clothe. Spanish then did something economical: it reached for the past participle of that verb — the form meaning having been clothed — and let it stand up on its own as a noun. A \textbf{vestido} is, in its bones, a clothed-thing. The garment is named after the act that put it on.

English borrowed the verb instead of the participle, and borrowed it more than once:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a \textbf{vest} came through French and Italian \emph{veste};
  \item to \textbf{invest} was \emph{investīre}, to clothe someone in an office — the cloth is still there in a bishop's investiture;
  \item to \textbf{divest} is to strip that clothing back off;
  \item a \textbf{travesty} is Italian \emph{travestīre}, to dress across, meaning a disguise, and then a grotesque imitation of the thing disguised.
\end{itemize}

The money sense of \textbf{invest} came later, out of Italian banking: you clothe your capital in something. The ceremony came first.

One label that looks like family and is not. \textbf{Transvestite} was coined in German in 1910, by Magnus Hirschfeld, out of Latin parts. That is modern manufacture, not a word handed down.

And the quiet cousin is one you use daily without noticing: to \textbf{wear}. It comes down the Germanic line from the same ancient root the Romans built \emph{vestis} on — grown alongside Latin rather than borrowed from it.

The trap: \emph{un vestido} is a dress. It is not a vest.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name a garment by the act that put it on: \emph{el vestido}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el vestido}
  \item \emph{un vestido nuevo}
  \item \emph{el vestido de la fiesta}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What form of \emph{vestīre} is \emph{vestido}? (The past participle — the clothed one.) And what did \emph{invest} mean before money got involved? (To clothe a person in an office.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el zapato]{el zapato — the shoe nobody can trace}

\label{lesson:ES-C360-zapato}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the clothes}, then \emph{the dress}. (\emph{La ropa}; \emph{el vestido}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el pie — the part of you this goes on.
  \item caminar — what you do once it is on.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sa-PA-to}, three beats with the weight on the middle one. Across most of the Spanish-speaking world the \emph{z} is said as a clear \emph{s}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el zapato} — \textquotedblleft{}the shoe.\textquotedblright{}

Nearly every word you have met has a paper trail. This one has none.

\emph{Zapato} has relatives everywhere. Portuguese says \emph{sapato}. Catalan and Occitan say \emph{sabata}. French has \emph{savate}, a worn-out old shoe — and the name of a kicking sport. Italian has \emph{ciabatta}, which means an old slipper and also a bread, the loaf being named for the same flat floppy shape. Arabic has \emph{sabbat}. A shoe-word ran across the western Mediterranean and settled in languages that are not related to each other.

Where did it start? Corominas, who spent a career on Spanish etymology, could not resolve it. A Turkic or Iranian source gets proposed from time to time, but that is speculation rather than a finding. The honest answer is that the trail goes cold.

There is one more thing to unlearn here, and it is famous. You have probably heard that \textbf{sabotage} comes from French workers hurling wooden shoes into machinery to wreck it. It does not. French \emph{saboter} meant to bungle a job, or to clatter about noisily in clogs — careless, loud, useless work. The shoe-in-the-gears tale was assembled in the twentieth century and no document supports it.

So this word teaches two things at once: a shoe that half a continent shares, and a beloved etymology that turns out to be a story people enjoyed telling.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name what goes on the foot, and you can name one famous etymology that is false: \emph{el zapato}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el zapato}
  \item \emph{un zapato nuevo}
  \item \emph{los zapatos y la ropa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \emph{zapato} come from? (Nobody has managed to trace it.) And what is wrong with the wooden-shoe account of \emph{sabotage}? (It was invented in the twentieth century; \emph{saboter} meant to bungle a job or clatter about in clogs.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el pantalón]{el pantalón — the trousers named after a stage character}

\label{lesson:ES-C360-pantalon}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the dress}, then \emph{the shoe}. (\emph{El vestido}; \emph{el zapato}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la pierna — the part of you this goes on.
  \item la rodilla — the joint the old kind of legwear stopped at.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pan-ta-LON}, three beats with the weight on the last one — the accent mark is there to say so. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el pantalón} — \textquotedblleft{}trousers.\textquotedblright{}

This garment is named after a man who never existed.

The Venetian comic stage worked from a small cast of fixed characters, and one of them was \textbf{Pantalone}: an old miser, forever scheming, forever outwitted. His costume was as fixed as his temper, and its memorable feature was his legwear — long, narrow, running the whole way down to the foot, at a time when other men's legwear stopped at the knee. Audiences began calling that style by his name.

French took the character's name over as \textbf{pantalon}, meaning the garment itself. Spanish took the word from French in the seventeen hundreds.

Where did the character get his own name? The usual account sends it to \textbf{San Pantaleone}, a saint with a strong following in Venice. \emph{Pantaleon} is Greek: \emph{pan-}, all, plus \emph{leon}, lion. That step is an inference from Venetian naming habits rather than a documented handover, so hold it lightly. The Greek pieces themselves are solid — \emph{pan-} is the \emph{pan-} of \textbf{panorama}, and \emph{leon} is the lion inside the name \textbf{Leonard}.

English walked the same road at the same time. \textbf{Pantaloons} came in whole, then got clipped down to \textbf{pants}. So the word printed on the label of your trousers and \emph{el pantalón} are one word wearing two lengths.

A small habit worth copying: Spanish is content with \emph{un pantalón}, one of them, where English insists on a plural pair.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name the garment for the legs, and say it in the singular the way Spanish prefers: \emph{el pantalón}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el pantalón}
  \item \emph{un pantalón nuevo}
  \item \emph{el pantalón y el zapato}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Who was Pantalone? (A stock character of the Venetian comic stage, whose long tight legwear got named after him.) And which English word is the same word, clipped short? (\emph{Pants}, from \emph{pantaloons}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el botón]{el botón — the fastener that is still a bud}

\label{lesson:ES-C360-boton}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the shoe}, then \emph{the trousers}. (\emph{El zapato}; \emph{el pantalón}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la mano — what you need to work one.
  \item la flor — the other thing this word names.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bo-TON}, two beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{b} is soft here, the lips barely closing on it. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el botón} — \textquotedblleft{}the button.\textquotedblright{}

Start with the verb, not the noun. Old French \textbf{bouter} meant to thrust, to push, to shove; French had taken it from a Germanic word, \textbf{bōtan}, to strike. Out of that verb came the noun \textbf{boton}: a thing that pushes out.

Notice what that describes. It is a shape, not a job. It says nothing about fastening, nothing about cloth. It says only: this sticks out.

Which is why one word covers two objects that resemble each other in no other way. A \textbf{botón} on a shirt sticks out. And a \textbf{botón} on a rose bush — a bud, tight and rounded, pushing its way out of the stem — sticks out in precisely the same manner. Spanish was never asked to choose between the two, and Old French was not either; \emph{boton} carried both from the beginning.

The pushing surfaces all over English:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a \textbf{buttress} pushes back against a leaning wall;
  \item to \textbf{rebut} is to push a claim back at the person making it;
  \item to \textbf{abut} is to push up against;
  \item a goat \textbf{butts} you: it strikes, with its head.
\end{itemize}

And \textbf{beat} is the cousin that came down the Germanic line rather than through France — the same striking, inherited instead of borrowed.

A caution, because English is untidy here. The other \textbf{butt}s — a barrel, the butt of a joke, the one you sit on — are separate words with separate histories. Only the striking one belongs to this family.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can name the thing on your shirt and the bud on a stem with one word: \emph{el botón}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el botón}
  \item \emph{un botón nuevo}
  \item \emph{el botón de la flor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{bouter} mean? (To thrust or push.) And why does \emph{botón} also name a flower bud? (Because the word means a thing that juts out, and a bud does exactly that.)
\end{tcolorbox}
